items.reason: "In what ecstatic ether does the world sail, the one that even the weariest will never tire of?" -- 'the one' can attach to 'ether' instead of 'world'; the relative clause must point clearly at the world.
items.new: Oh, grassy glades! Oh, endless landscapes of everlasting spring in the soul! In you — though you have long been parched by the dead drought of our earthy life — in you men can still roll like young horses in fresh morning clover, and for a few fleeting moments feel the cool dew of immortal life on them. I wish to God these blessed calms would last. But the mingled and mingling threads of life are woven warp and woof: calms crossed by storms, a storm for every calm. There is no steady progress in this life that never doubles back; we do not climb through fixed stages and then rest at the last one. We pass through infancy's unconscious spell, boyhood's unthinking faith, adolescence's doubt (the common fate), then skepticism, then disbelief, and come to rest at last in manhood's brooding repose of If. But once we have gone through it all, we go round the circle again, and are infants, boys and men, and Ifs, forever. Where is the final harbor, from which we will never cast off again? In what ecstatic ether does that world sail — the world that even the weariest will never tire of? Where is the foundling's father hidden? Our souls are like those orphans whose unmarried mothers die giving birth to them: the secret of who our father is lies in their grave, and we must go there to learn it.

Now, decked out in cheerful holiday finery, she was sailing joyfully — if a little boastfully — around among the widely scattered ships on the cruising ground before turning her prow for home.

items.new: The season for the Line, the equator, finally came close. Every day, whenever Ahab came up from his cabin and looked aloft, the watchful helmsman would make a show of handling his spokes, and the eager sailors would hurry to the braces and stand there with every eye fixed on the nailed doubloon, impatient for the order to point the ship's prow toward the equator. In due time the order came. It was nearly high noon, and Ahab, seated in the bow of his boat, which was hoisted high, was about to take his usual daily sighting of the sun to find his latitude.

items.new: "What is it, what nameless, inscrutable, unearthly thing is it; what deceitful, hidden lord and master, what cruel, remorseless emperor commands me, so that against all natural loves and longings I keep pushing and crowding and jamming myself on all the time, recklessly making myself ready to do what in my own proper, natural heart I would not dare so much as to dare? Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm? But if the great sun does not move by himself, but is like an errand-boy in heaven; and if not one single star can revolve except by some invisible power; how then can this one small heart beat, this one small brain think thoughts, unless God does that beating, does that thinking, does that living, and not I? By heaven, man, we are turned round and round in this world like that windlass over there, and Fate is the handspike. And all the while, look! that smiling sky, and this unsounded sea! Look! See that albacore there! Who put it into him to chase that flying-fish and sink his fangs in it? Where do murderers go, man? Who is to pass sentence, when the judge himself is dragged before the bar? But it is a mild, mild wind, and a mild-looking sky; and the air smells now as if it blew from a faraway meadow; they have been making hay somewhere under the slopes of the Andes, Starbuck, and the mowers are sleeping in the new-mown hay. Sleeping? Aye, however hard we toil, we all sleep in the field at last. Sleep? Aye, and rust amid the green, like last year's scythes thrown down and left in the half-cut rows — Starbuck!"
